evidence.quote:
The October flash all-industry PMI continued to point to robust business activity 
at the start of the fourth quarter, even as the output measure edged down to 57.6 
from 58.4 in September. Despite the moderation, this marked the second-highest 
reading for the composite output index since March 2022. The press release 
estimated that the latest survey data are consistent with annualized GDP growth of 
around 5%, following growth of roughly 4% indicated for 3Q. That is quite a bit 
stronger than our forecast for a moderation back to 1.75% growth this quarter. The 
surveys suggest that growth remains slightly more services-led, with the services 
business activity index easing to 57.9 from 58.8 and the manufacturing output 
index declining to 55.8 from 56.2.
The details of the report continued to suggest that demand is running ahead of 
firms’ operating capacity. Composite new orders accelerated to their fastest pace 
in more than four and a half years, as stronger growth in services demand more than 
offset some moderation in manufacturing orders. Export demand also improved, 
with the all-industry index posting its strongest increase since May 2022. At the 
same time, backlogs of work rose by the most since May 2022, with unfinished 
business accumulating at a faster pace in both manufacturing and services. 
Supplier delivery times also lengthened to the greatest extent since 2022 amid 
material and labor shortages, low inventory levels, overloaded suppliers, and 
shipping and import delays. The press release noted that some of the strength in 
demand may have reflected precautionary inventory building. Manufacturing 
input inventories rose at their fastest pace in four months.
The PMI employment gauges also remained strong in October. The all-industry 
employment index came in at its second-highest level in more than four years, 
surpassed only by September’s reading. Firms continued to expand capacity in 
response to stronger demand. The survey’s gauge of manufacturing employment 
growth accelerated to its highest level since March 2012. Service-sector hiring 
moderated from September but remained at one of its highest levels in more than 
four years. The combination of strong hiring and rising backlogs suggests that 
firms remain focused on adding headcount, although reported labor shortages 
continue to pose constraints. While the September employment report came in a 
little softer than expected, we still anticipate a pickup in hiring in the months ahead.
evidence.title: US: Flash PMI signals robust growth at the start of 4Q

evidence.quote:
The inflation signal from the PMIs pointed to a further intensification of price pressures. The 
all-industry input cost index held at an elevated 64.9, its second-highest reading since 
November 2022. Respondents cited higher energy, fuel, freight, and raw-material costs, 
including steel, aluminum, and copper, alongside higher wages, utilities, and insurance costs. 
The output price PMI, meanwhile, rose a further 1.5 points to 59.8, its highest reading since 
August 2022. The pickup was broad-based, with services prices rising at their fastest pace 
since August 2022 and manufacturing selling prices increasing at the strongest rate since July 
2022. Business expectations for the year ahead moderated from September but remained the 
second highest so far this year, as stronger manufacturing confidence partly offset softer 
sentiment among service-sector providers.

Comments from Fed officials in recent weeks have pointed to a compromise to 
n
hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate 
unchanged today at its October meeting.  The meeting provided little new 
information and little reason to think that the FOMC will deviate from that plan 
anytime soon.  We continue to expect a second and final hike in December.  A 
third hike in March is also possible if inflation comes in higher than we expect. 
We saw Chairman Warsh’s comments as balanced and broadly consistent with 
n
both a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of rate hikes.  
Warsh emphasized the strength of the economy and the labor market but said 
that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but 
are not tight.

As widely expected, the BoJ kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.25%. The 
dissenting vote came from Takata, who called for a rate hike. Although the policy 
rate was left unchanged, the BoJ unanimously decided to accelerate the pace of its 
ETF sales, increasing the pace from the current book-value-based annual rate of 
JPY330 billion to JPY860 billion, effective from January 2027. As a result, the 
number of years required to complete the sale will be shortened from the previously 
expected approximately 112 years to approximately 43 years. The changes to the 
Outlook Report forecasts were also largely in line with prior expectations, with the 
BoJ making small upward revisions to its FY26 growth outlook and its FY27 and 
FY28 inflation outlooks.
The focus of attention was the BoJ’s judgment on underlying inflation. The BoJ 
judged, for the first time, that “Underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally 
consistent with the price stability target of 2%,” while maintaining that near-term 
inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. Amid this, the BoJ continues to hold 
the view that financial conditions remain accommodative. The views expressed in 
the Outlook Report imply that the current inflation environment justifies a 
neutralization of the policy rate, and that the 1.25% policy rate is likely not yet at 
a neutral level. This is consistent with our view that the BoJ will continue to raise 
rates at a roughly quarterly pace for the time being.

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

previously) and +0.1% growth ex. Ireland. Our inflation nearcasts for end-2026 were 
little changed today.

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

BOTTOM LINE: At the area-wide level, real GDP rose by +0.42%qoq in Q3. Excluding

previously) and +0.1% growth ex. Ireland. Our inflation nearcasts for end-2026 were 
little changed today.

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate

information and little reason to think that the FOMC will deviate from that plan

both a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of rate hikes.

that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but 
are not tight.

the fastest gain in a year. Private domestic final sales rose even quicker, 4.9%, and 
over two quarters the average 4.8% pace in this category is the best in more than

that include the OBBBA tax stimulus earlier this year, AI capex, large gains in 
household wealth, and household willingness to reduce saving rates. We still 
expect slower growth this quarter, and are leaving our 4Q GDP forecast at 1.75%, 
though strong October PMIs point to some upside risk there.

further risk-off developments lead to no additional hikes this cycle.

evidence.quote:
According to the Bank of Korea’s survey, the consumer sentiment index (CSI) fell 
by 1.2 points to 105.4 in October, retracing roughly half of the September rebound 
(Figure 1). The monthly decline was broad-based across major sub-indices, except 
for the household living conditions index. Given that the survey was conducted 
from October 13-20, the print likely reflects consumer concerns over renewed 
energy price pressures and less supportive asset effects from the domestic stock 
market. This suggests balanced risks for 4Q private consumption growth, though 
we continue to see gradual improvement in labor and income conditions.

We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour

coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate

that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but 
are not tight.

are not tight.

over two quarters the average 4.8% pace in this category is the best in more than

that include the OBBBA tax stimulus earlier this year, AI capex, large gains in

though strong October PMIs point to some upside risk there.

Chair Warsh dovishly noted that higher policy rates are having their 
expected effect in tightening financial conditions and acknowledged that 
policy rates may already be at appropriate settings. He also limited the 
scope of rate hikes next year by reducing the number of “live” meetings from 
eight to seven (which will drop to six in 2028). We continue to think Warsh 
is overstating the breadth of strength in the US economy, meaning he will 
likely have a relatively low-bar for a downside surprise. In our base case, the 
Fed hikes another 25bp in December, but it wouldn’t be too surprising if 
further risk-off developments lead to no additional hikes this cycle.

evidence.quote:
Comments from Fed officials in recent weeks have pointed to a compromise to 
n
hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate 
unchanged today at its October meeting.  The meeting provided little new 
information and little reason to think that the FOMC will deviate from that plan 
anytime soon.  We continue to expect a second and final hike in December.  A 
third hike in March is also possible if inflation comes in higher than we expect. 
We saw Chairman Warsh’s comments as balanced and broadly consistent with 
n
both a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of rate hikes.  
Warsh emphasized the strength of the economy and the labor market but said 
that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but 
are not tight.

evidence.quote:
Real GDP rose at a brisk 3.4%q/q saar pace in 3Q (JPMC and consensus: 3.2%), 
the fastest gain in a year. Private domestic final sales rose even quicker, 4.9%, and 
over two quarters the average 4.8% pace in this category is the best in more than 
a decade (ex-COVID). This is despite a large energy price shock, reflecting offsets 
that include the OBBBA tax stimulus earlier this year, AI capex, large gains in 
household wealth, and household willingness to reduce saving rates. We still 
expect slower growth this quarter, and are leaving our 4Q GDP forecast at 1.75%, 
though strong October PMIs point to some upside risk there.

Chair Warsh dovishly noted that higher policy rates are having their 
expected effect in tightening financial conditions and acknowledged that 
policy rates may already be at appropriate settings. He also limited the 
scope of rate hikes next year by reducing the number of “live” meetings from 
eight to seven (which will drop to six in 2028). We continue to think Warsh

further risk-off developments lead to no additional hikes this cycle.

Following the 3Q CPI data and recent RBA commentary, we now expect the 
bank to tighten policy by a further 25bp at this week's meeting. Recent speeches 
from RBA officials reversed the message from September’s press conference, 
suggesting inflation is not yet under control and there is still work to do. The 
3Q CPI data were consistent with this shift, pushing market pricing towards a 
~90% chance of a hike. We think further rate hikes beyond the November 
meeting are unlikely given the weakness in the activity data (GDP and 
unemployment), but with inflation still too high, the RBA will retain its 
hawkish bias and reiterate that "the Board will continue to do what it considers 
necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the 
cash rate target further if needed."

evidence.quote:
Hike to 4.85% given persistent inflation concerns 
We expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 and 
retain a tightening bias. Recent RBA communications have clearly signalled that a hike is 
likely, with inflation still too high and having remained above the target band for too 
long. Near-term inflation forecasts are also likely to be revised higher, while a 
reassessment of the RBA’s NAIRU suggests a tighter labour market than previously 
thought (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2). However, we expect a split vote as Deputy Governor 
Hauser’s observation that “we’re in a world of hard choices” highlights the increasingly 
difficult policy trade-off. We expect some MPB members to vote for a hold to allow 
more time to assess the cyclical slowdown and the cumulative impact of earlier 
tightening. 
Risk skew dovish, watch for split vote & dovish presser 
Market pricing for the November meeting is around 20bp, with 31bp priced by February, 
which seems reasonable to us. Our base case is for the RBA to retain a tightening bias 
amid elevated energy prices but risks are skewed towards a more dovish outcome than 
is priced beyond Nov RBA. While a substantial upward revision remains the main hawkish 
risk and could lead markets to fully price another hike by February, in our view markets 
have already priced upward revisions to the RBA’s NAIRU estimate and inflation 
forecasts. On the other hand, a close vote (5-4 or 6-3) or a dovish presser (Gov. Bullock 
emphasising weaker labour market trends), bringing forward market expectations for 
easing to H1 ‘27. We see AU rates outperforming US, especially in the long end, but 
remain wary of front-end longs at this stage given the upside risks to Oct CPI from the 
impact of a credit card surcharge ban.

Following the 3Q CPI data and recent RBA commentary, we now expect the 
bank to tighten policy by a further 25bp at this week's meeting. Recent speeches 
from RBA officials reversed the message from September’s press conference, 
suggesting inflation is not yet under control and there is still work to do. The 
3Q CPI data were consistent with this shift, pushing market pricing towards a 
~90% chance of a hike. We think further rate hikes beyond the November 
meeting are unlikely given the weakness in the activity data (GDP and 
unemployment), but with inflation still too high, the RBA will retain its 
hawkish bias and reiterate that "the Board will continue to do what it considers 
necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the 
cash rate target further if needed."

evidence.quote:
Hike to 4.85% given persistent inflation concerns 
We expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 and 
retain a tightening bias. Recent RBA communications have clearly signalled that a hike is 
likely, with inflation still too high and having remained above the target band for too 
long. Near-term inflation forecasts are also likely to be revised higher, while a 
reassessment of the RBA’s NAIRU suggests a tighter labour market than previously 
thought (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2). However, we expect a split vote as Deputy Governor 
Hauser’s observation that “we’re in a world of hard choices” highlights the increasingly 
difficult policy trade-off. We expect some MPB members to vote for a hold to allow 
more time to assess the cyclical slowdown and the cumulative impact of earlier 
tightening. 
Risk skew dovish, watch for split vote & dovish presser 
Market pricing for the November meeting is around 20bp, with 31bp priced by February, 
which seems reasonable to us. Our base case is for the RBA to retain a tightening bias 
amid elevated energy prices but risks are skewed towards a more dovish outcome than 
is priced beyond Nov RBA. While a substantial upward revision remains the main hawkish 
risk and could lead markets to fully price another hike by February, in our view markets 
have already priced upward revisions to the RBA’s NAIRU estimate and inflation 
forecasts. On the other hand, a close vote (5-4 or 6-3) or a dovish presser (Gov. Bullock 
emphasising weaker labour market trends), bringing forward market expectations for 
easing to H1 ‘27. We see AU rates outperforming US, especially in the long end, but 
remain wary of front-end longs at this stage given the upside risks to Oct CPI from the 
impact of a credit card surcharge ban.

evidence.quote:
Hike to 4.85% given persistent inflation concerns 
We expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 and 
retain a tightening bias. Recent RBA communications have clearly signalled that a hike is 
likely, with inflation still too high and having remained above the target band for too 
long. Near-term inflation forecasts are also likely to be revised higher, while a 
reassessment of the RBA’s NAIRU suggests a tighter labour market than previously 
thought (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2). However, we expect a split vote as Deputy Governor 
Hauser’s observation that “we’re in a world of hard choices” highlights the increasingly 
difficult policy trade-off. We expect some MPB members to vote for a hold to allow 
more time to assess the cyclical slowdown and the cumulative impact of earlier 
tightening. 
Risk skew dovish, watch for split vote & dovish presser 
Market pricing for the November meeting is around 20bp, with 31bp priced by February, 
which seems reasonable to us. Our base case is for the RBA to retain a tightening bias 
amid elevated energy prices but risks are skewed towards a more dovish outcome than 
is priced beyond Nov RBA. While a substantial upward revision remains the main hawkish 
risk and could lead markets to fully price another hike by February, in our view markets 
have already priced upward revisions to the RBA’s NAIRU estimate and inflation 
forecasts. On the other hand, a close vote (5-4 or 6-3) or a dovish presser (Gov. Bullock 
emphasising weaker labour market trends), bringing forward market expectations for 
easing to H1 ‘27. We see AU rates outperforming US, especially in the long end, but 
remain wary of front-end longs at this stage given the upside risks to Oct CPI from the 
impact of a credit card surcharge ban.

evidence.quote:
Hike to 4.85% given persistent inflation concerns 
We expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 and 
retain a tightening bias. Recent RBA communications have clearly signalled that a hike is 
likely, with inflation still too high and having remained above the target band for too 
long. Near-term inflation forecasts are also likely to be revised higher, while a 
reassessment of the RBA’s NAIRU suggests a tighter labour market than previously 
thought (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2). However, we expect a split vote as Deputy Governor 
Hauser’s observation that “we’re in a world of hard choices” highlights the increasingly 
difficult policy trade-off. We expect some MPB members to vote for a hold to allow 
more time to assess the cyclical slowdown and the cumulative impact of earlier 
tightening. 
Risk skew dovish, watch for split vote & dovish presser 
Market pricing for the November meeting is around 20bp, with 31bp priced by February, 
which seems reasonable to us. Our base case is for the RBA to retain a tightening bias 
amid elevated energy prices but risks are skewed towards a more dovish outcome than 
is priced beyond Nov RBA. While a substantial upward revision remains the main hawkish 
risk and could lead markets to fully price another hike by February, in our view markets 
have already priced upward revisions to the RBA’s NAIRU estimate and inflation 
forecasts. On the other hand, a close vote (5-4 or 6-3) or a dovish presser (Gov. Bullock 
emphasising weaker labour market trends), bringing forward market expectations for 
easing to H1 ‘27. We see AU rates outperforming US, especially in the long end, but 
remain wary of front-end longs at this stage given the upside risks to Oct CPI from the 
impact of a credit card surcharge ban.

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

evidence.quote:
Comments from Fed officials in recent weeks have pointed to a compromise to 
n
hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate 
unchanged today at its October meeting.  The meeting provided little new 
information and little reason to think that the FOMC will deviate from that plan 
anytime soon.  We continue to expect a second and final hike in December.  A 
third hike in March is also possible if inflation comes in higher than we expect. 
We saw Chairman Warsh’s comments as balanced and broadly consistent with 
n
both a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of rate hikes.  
Warsh emphasized the strength of the economy and the labor market but said 
that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but

evidence.quote:
The BoC hikes 25bp to 2.50% 
The Bank of Canada (BoC) raised its policy rate 25bp to 2.50% at its October 28 
meeting, contrary to our expectations (E: 2.50%, BofA: 2.25%). This was the BoC's first 
hike in more than three years. The BoC pointed to rising inflation risks from elevated 
energy prices and from high import costs that are passing through to prices. It also said 
new US tariffs have added uncertainty to the growth outlook. 
BoC sees higher inflation risks… 
The BoC now expects inflation to be “higher and more persistent” than in the July 
Monetary Policy Report (MPR). Higher-for-longer energy prices and greater cost pass-
through are adding to inflation persistence. Businesses have largely absorbed higher 
input costs so far. However, the BoC expects pass-through to increase over the next 
year, which raises the risk that higher fuel and imported input costs spill over more 
broadly into consumer prices. The BoC now sees CPI inflation rising to about 3.5% by 
end-2026 and averaging 3% in 2027, 1pp above the July projection, before returning to 
2% around mid-2028. Our forecast has inflation at 2.8% by end-2026 and 2.0% by end-
2027, with upside risks. That means faster disinflation than the BoC expects. 
… but growth prospects are more uncertain  
The BoC now expects GDP growth of 1.0% in 2026 and 2.0% in both 2027 and 2028, a 
somewhat stronger projection overall than in the July MPR (BofA: 1.0% in 2026 and 1.6% 
in 2027). Still, the Bank continues to flag considerable uncertainty around the outlook, 
particularly regarding Canada-US trade relations. In our view, the direct impact of higher 
tariffs is likely limited because they cover a narrow share of exports. The bigger concern 
is that prolonged trade uncertainty weighs on investment and hiring (see report). 
BoC: one more hike, but not until January 
The BoC kept a tightening bias, noting that there could be a need to increase the policy 
rate further, but said it would proceed carefully given uncertainties. We now expect one 
more hike in January and look for the BoC to stay on hold in December. We see two 
reasons for the BoC to skip December. First, the economy is likely to decelerate in 4Q, 
which the BoC already expects. Second, we think the BoC's new year-end inflation 
forecast of 3.5% is too high, given that inflation was 3.1% in September. Risks to our 
call point to an earlier and larger tightening cycle: the hike could come in December 
instead of January, and depending on oil, the BoC could end up hiking more than once.

evidence.quote:
Implications 
Today’s widely anticipated decision supports our base case that the BoJ will remain on hold at the 
final Monetary Policy Meeting (MPM) of the year on 18 December, deliver one further 25bp rate increase 
on 22 January 2027 to 1.50%, and then keep rates unchanged thereafter. 
The BoJ also announced a unanimous decision today to accelerate its exchange-traded fund (ETF) sales. 
It plans to sell around JPY860bn of ETFs per year on a book-value basis, equivalent to 0.1% of market 
trading value. At this pace, the BoJ could complete its ETF sales in 43 years, compared with the 112 years 
previously estimated in September 2025, when it began selling JPY330bn of holdings annually, equivalent 
to 0.05% of market trading value. In our view, this represents another step in the BoJ’s broader 
monetary policy normalisation campaign by reducing its large balance sheet. 
Pressure on the BoJ to accelerate monetary tightening continues to build. As we highlighted in our 
preview note, the risks to our base case of a January 2027 hike increasingly point towards an earlier move 
at the December 2026 MPM. The BoJ faces pressure to keep pace with the US Federal Reserve, which 
raised rates at the September FOMC meeting. HSBC US economist Ryan Wang expects a further 25bp 
increase in December 2026, while a wider Japan–US policy-rate differential could renew pressure on the 
yen (see FOMC Multi-Asset Reaction: Skip today, hike tomorrow, 28 October 2026).

Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes

ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is

increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by 
0.9% q-o-q. Investment recorded a 0.1% q-o-q gain. Meanwhile, net trade contributed 0.1ppts to 
growth; both exports and imports increased on the quarter. 
 
 
◆ Eurozone growth slowed less than expected, GDP up 0.4% q-o-q in Q3 as 
France disappointed but Germany surprised to the upside 
◆ While ever-volatile Ireland added 0.2ppts to growth, country commentary 
points to overall domestic demand resilience but export payback 
◆  Stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB is on track for more hikes
evidence.title: Eurozone GDP (Q3, 1st release) Defying headwinds, albeit boosted by Ireland

evidence.quote:
Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

evidence.quote:
Facts 
Eurozone GDP grew by 0.4% q-o-q in the provisional release for Q3 2026, twice the pace Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for (HSBC: 0.2% q-o-q). This was a deceleration relative to the 0.6% 
recorded in Q2.  
The headline overstates the strength however as Irish GDP was up 5.5% on the quarter, adding 0.2ppts to 
total eurozone growth. Excluding Ireland, growth would have been 0.2% q-o-q, the same as in Q2. 
On an annual basis, the eurozone expanded by 1.3% compared to 1.2% recorded in the prior quarter.  
The preliminary flash release doesn’t contain a breakdown of growth by expenditure, but country-level 
data and commentary point to consumer resilience on the one hand and export payback on the other. Full 
expenditure details will be available in the third release on 7 December.  
Across the big 4 economies: 
◆ Germany surprised to the upside, with the third quarter growth coming in at 0.2% q-o-q (Bloomberg 
consensus: +0.1% q-o-q, HSBC: 0.0% q-o-q), following +0.3% q-o-q in Q2. No detailed estimates 
were published with the flash print, but Destatis mentioned that consumption expenditure was up 
while investment declined, and exports had slowed noticeably compared to H1. 
◆ In France, activity unexpectedly shrunk by 0.1% q-o-q following a flat second quarter. Bloomberg 
consensus had been looking for a small plus (0.1% q-o-q). The decline reflected a fall in exports and 
investment while consumer spending (+0.4% q-o-q) and public consumption (+0.3% q-o-q) were 
relatively firm (French GDP (Q3 26, 1st release), 30 October). 
◆ Italy’s GDP was flat, following 0.2% q-o-q in Q2, in an undershoot to Bloomberg consensus 
expectations (0.1% q-o-q). Istat noted a positive contribution from domestic demand – including 
changes of inventories – and a drag from net exports. A full breakdown is published on 1 December. 
◆ Spanish GDP growth eased from 0.7% q-o-q in Q2 to 0.6% q-o-q in Q3, in line with Bloomberg 
consensus expectations. Annual growth ticked up to 2.7%. The preliminary breakdown showed strong 
domestic demand: household consumption was up by 0.5% q-o-q and government consumption by

Comments from Fed officials in recent weeks have pointed to a compromise to 
n
hike every other meeting.  Consistent with that, the FOMC left the funds rate

information and little reason to think that the FOMC will deviate from that plan 
anytime soon.  We continue to expect a second and final hike in December.  A

both a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of rate hikes.

that neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was 
running too hot.  He noted that inflation compensation and inflation 
expectations had moved in the right direction.  And he said that raising interest 
rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but 
are not tight.

household wealth, and household willingness to reduce saving rates. We still 
expect slower growth this quarter, and are leaving our 4Q GDP forecast at 1.75%, 
though strong October PMIs point to some upside risk there.

Chair Warsh dovishly noted that higher policy rates are having their

eight to seven (which will drop to six in 2028). We continue to think Warsh 
is overstating the breadth of strength in the US economy, meaning he will 
likely have a relatively low-bar for a downside surprise. In our base case, the 
Fed hikes another 25bp in December, but it wouldn’t be too surprising if 
further risk-off developments lead to no additional hikes this cycle.

though strong October PMIs point to some upside risk there.

Chair Warsh dovishly noted that higher policy rates are having their 
expected effect in tightening financial conditions and acknowledged that 
policy rates may already be at appropriate settings. He also limited the 
scope of rate hikes next year by reducing the number of “live” meetings from 
eight to seven (which will drop to six in 2028). We continue to think Warsh 
is overstating the breadth of strength in the US economy, meaning he will 
likely have a relatively low-bar for a downside surprise. In our base case, the 
Fed hikes another 25bp in December, but it wouldn’t be too surprising if 
further risk-off developments lead to no additional hikes this cycle.

We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

Dovish undertones as expected, even in writing 
We did get the dovish undertones we were expecting. Additionally, we got some of them 
in the statement, which gives them more weight: 1) an emphasis on the good behaviour 
of underlying inflation and wages; 2) a lot more emphasis on the downside to growth 
coming from energy and financing conditions; and 3) despite the increase in energy 
prices, a "measured approach" remains appropriate (i.e. a short hiking cycle).  
It takes surprises to stop a Dec hike though 
The press conference emphasized those dovish points again for most of the discussion. 
But, as we expected, there was also the need to keep a hiking bias for December. And 
ECB President Lagarde made that clear when she argued that the direction of travel is 
clear, absent surprises. That statement (i.e. the hiking bias) was repeated several times, 
which undid part of the initial dovish market reaction.  
Our call remains unchanged, but risk balance shifted 
Where does this leave our ECB call? With no changes other than in the balance of risks. 
We expect one final hike in December. Another hike in March is a possibility but looks 
increasingly difficult as long as financial conditions remain tight and second-round 
effects are almost absent. A hold in December is not unthinkable, in our view, if activity 
data deteriorates more than expected, financial conditions remain this tight, core 
inflation doesn’t move much, and second-round effects do not surprise.

As widely expected, the BoJ kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.25%. The 
dissenting vote came from Takata, who called for a rate hike. Although the policy 
rate was left unchanged, the BoJ unanimously decided to accelerate the pace of its 
ETF sales, increasing the pace from the current book-value-based annual rate of 
JPY330 billion to JPY860 billion, effective from January 2027. As a result, the 
number of years required to complete the sale will be shortened from the previously 
expected approximately 112 years to approximately 43 years. The changes to the 
Outlook Report forecasts were also largely in line with prior expectations, with the 
BoJ making small upward revisions to its FY26 growth outlook and its FY27 and 
FY28 inflation outlooks.
The focus of attention was the BoJ’s judgment on underlying inflation. The BoJ 
judged, for the first time, that “Underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally 
consistent with the price stability target of 2%,” while maintaining that near-term 
inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. Amid this, the BoJ continues to hold 
the view that financial conditions remain accommodative. The views expressed in 
the Outlook Report imply that the current inflation environment justifies a 
neutralization of the policy rate, and that the 1.25% policy rate is likely not yet at 
a neutral level. This is consistent with our view that the BoJ will continue to raise 
rates at a roughly quarterly pace for the time being.

evidence.quote:
As widely expected, the BoJ kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.25%. The 
dissenting vote came from Takata, who called for a rate hike. Although the policy 
rate was left unchanged, the BoJ unanimously decided to accelerate the pace of its 
ETF sales, increasing the pace from the current book-value-based annual rate of 
JPY330 billion to JPY860 billion, effective from January 2027. As a result, the 
number of years required to complete the sale will be shortened from the previously 
expected approximately 112 years to approximately 43 years. The changes to the 
Outlook Report forecasts were also largely in line with prior expectations, with the 
BoJ making small upward revisions to its FY26 growth outlook and its FY27 and 
FY28 inflation outlooks.
The focus of attention was the BoJ’s judgment on underlying inflation. The BoJ 
judged, for the first time, that “Underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally 
consistent with the price stability target of 2%,” while maintaining that near-term 
inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. Amid this, the BoJ continues to hold 
the view that financial conditions remain accommodative. The views expressed in 
the Outlook Report imply that the current inflation environment justifies a 
neutralization of the policy rate, and that the 1.25% policy rate is likely not yet at 
a neutral level. This is consistent with our view that the BoJ will continue to raise 
rates at a roughly quarterly pace for the time being.
evidence.title: BoJ: Target achieved, neutral in sight

evidence.quote:
As widely expected, the BoJ kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.25%. The 
dissenting vote came from Takata, who called for a rate hike. Although the policy 
rate was left unchanged, the BoJ unanimously decided to accelerate the pace of its 
ETF sales, increasing the pace from the current book-value-based annual rate of 
JPY330 billion to JPY860 billion, effective from January 2027. As a result, the 
number of years required to complete the sale will be shortened from the previously 
expected approximately 112 years to approximately 43 years. The changes to the 
Outlook Report forecasts were also largely in line with prior expectations, with the 
BoJ making small upward revisions to its FY26 growth outlook and its FY27 and 
FY28 inflation outlooks.
The focus of attention was the BoJ’s judgment on underlying inflation. The BoJ 
judged, for the first time, that “Underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally 
consistent with the price stability target of 2%,” while maintaining that near-term 
inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. Amid this, the BoJ continues to hold 
the view that financial conditions remain accommodative. The views expressed in 
the Outlook Report imply that the current inflation environment justifies a 
neutralization of the policy rate, and that the 1.25% policy rate is likely not yet at 
a neutral level. This is consistent with our view that the BoJ will continue to raise 
rates at a roughly quarterly pace for the time being.
evidence.title: BoJ: Target achieved, neutral in sight

Implications 
Today’s widely anticipated decision supports our base case that the BoJ will remain on hold at the 
final Monetary Policy Meeting (MPM) of the year on 18 December, deliver one further 25bp rate increase 
on 22 January 2027 to 1.50%, and then keep rates unchanged thereafter. 
The BoJ also announced a unanimous decision today to accelerate its exchange-traded fund (ETF) sales. 
It plans to sell around JPY860bn of ETFs per year on a book-value basis, equivalent to 0.1% of market 
trading value. At this pace, the BoJ could complete its ETF sales in 43 years, compared with the 112 years 
previously estimated in September 2025, when it began selling JPY330bn of holdings annually, equivalent 
to 0.05% of market trading value. In our view, this represents another step in the BoJ’s broader 
monetary policy normalisation campaign by reducing its large balance sheet. 
Pressure on the BoJ to accelerate monetary tightening continues to build. As we highlighted in our 
preview note, the risks to our base case of a January 2027 hike increasingly point towards an earlier move 
at the December 2026 MPM. The BoJ faces pressure to keep pace with the US Federal Reserve, which 
raised rates at the September FOMC meeting. HSBC US economist Ryan Wang expects a further 25bp 
increase in December 2026, while a wider Japan–US policy-rate differential could renew pressure on the 
yen (see FOMC Multi-Asset Reaction: Skip today, hike tomorrow, 28 October 2026).
